result: Curtaining propensity was systematically evaluated across four plasma gases (argon, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen) at different ion currents and voltages. Argon and xenon produced the smoothest surfaces with curtaining propensity under 10% at low currents (~0.2 nA), while nitrogen and oxygen exhibited greater curtaining. Argon showed lower curtaining than xenon at higher currents.
evaluation: Claims C37-C45 provide comprehensive experimental data on curtaining assessment with quantitative measurements across multiple conditions. The systematic comparison includes appropriate controls (different gases, currents, voltages) and quantitative scoring. The trend analysis and exceptions (e.g., nitrogen at 20 kV) are clearly documented with figure references.

result: Beam profiles of four plasma gases were characterized by measuring full width half maximum (FWHM) at different currents and voltages. Plasma sources showed considerably larger probe sizes than Ga-based sources. At 30 kV, argon had the smallest probe size, while at 20 kV all gases showed similar spot sizes with different plateau behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 describe systematic beam characterization with quantitative FWHM measurements. The comparison to Ga-based sources (C48) provides important context supported by citation. The voltage-dependent differences are clearly documented, though the biological implications of these differences could be better explored.

result: Imaging at 90° to the milled surface significantly improved image quality compared to 52° imaging. Resolution improved from 76±19 nm (52°) to 47±7 nm (90°), with immediately visible contrast enhancement. The improvement is attributed to differences in electron collection efficiency, which is maximal when normal to the SEM.
evaluation: Claims C74-C83 demonstrate clear improvement in imaging quality with quantitative resolution measurements using FRC analysis. The physical explanation (electron collection efficiency, C83) is supported by citation. Visual observations are corroborated by quantitative metrics. The requirement for stage movement (C75) and its minimal impact on drift (addressed in C84-C87) strengthen the result.

result: Stage movement for 90° imaging introduces minimal drift. XY shift increased from 52±38 nm (no movement) to 96±71 nm (with movement), representing <1% of FOV. Z-drift remained minimal (48.1±1.4 nm vs 48.9±4 nm for 50 nm target), confirming the 50 nm milling step is achievable under cryogenic conditions.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 provide quantitative assessment of stage movement effects with appropriate error estimates. The measurements demonstrate that the twofold increase in XY drift is negligible in absolute terms. Z-drift measurements confirm milling accuracy. The conclusion that stage movement does not significantly compromise data quality is well-supported.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of HeLa cells (500 slices, 50 nm depth) revealed various membranous compartments including nucleus, ER, mitochondria, and cristae. Two centrosomes with centriole pairs were observed, with spacing consistent with prophase (1.2 µm between centrosomes, 543 nm and 1561 nm between centriole pairs).
evaluation: Claims C57-C63 describe detailed cellular observations with quantitative measurements. The centrosome spacing and centriole measurements are supported by citations (C60, C61, C62) confirming biological interpretation. The negative observation (C63, no spindle microtubules) is appropriately reported. The resolution achieved allows visualization of these structures.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of HPF mouse brain cortex tissue (844.4 µm³ volume) revealed diverse cell types, myelinated neurons (diameter 0.53-2.8 µm), mitochondria with cristae (~87 total), and synaptic junctions with pre-synaptic vesicles (20-30 nm diameter). Synapse I contained ~184 vesicles, Synapse II ~98 vesicles, with diverse morphologies consistent with previous studies.
evaluation: Claims C64-C73 demonstrate the technique's capability for tissue imaging with extensive quantitative data. The observations span multiple scales from tissue organization to nanometer-scale vesicles. Quantitative counts and measurements are provided. Comparison to prior work (C73) validates the biological observations. The diversity of structures observed demonstrates the method's versatility.

result: Plunge-frozen R. rubrum imaged without stain or fixative revealed minimal artefacts and clear visualization of lipid droplets, inner/outer membranes (30-80 nm apart), and both mature (30-60 nm diameter) and nascent chromatophores. In 8 segmented cells, 2772 mature and 84 nascent chromatophores were observed, with nascent forms unevenly distributed (one cell with ~12% nascent, most with few or none). Data collection was accomplished in 2.5 hr automated.
evaluation: Claims C91-C103 demonstrate successful imaging of bacteria with quantitative analysis. The observation of nascent chromatophores budding from inner membrane (C98) is novel (C97). Quantitative segmentation data (C99) with extrapolation (C100) is reasonable. The uneven distribution observation (C101-C102) is biologically interesting and demonstrates the technique's ability to capture rare events (C103). Measurements are consistent with cited literature (C93, C96).

result: Vero cells milled with nitrogen plasma (worst performing gas) still revealed subcellular structures including 138 NPCs, mitochondrial networks, and membrane contact sites. Despite severe limitations (46 slices vs 500 for HeLa, 7 failed attempts), quantification showed 26 LD-ER contacts and 48 mitochondria-ER MCS with similar volumes (1-5 × 10⁻³ µm³) and Gaussian distribution, suggesting limits in ER tracking of organelles.
evaluation: Claims C104-C114 demonstrate that even the worst-performing gas can yield useful biological insights, though with significant technical challenges (C106-C107). The quantitative analysis of membrane contact sites (C111-C113) provides novel biological insight. The interpretation about ER tracking limits (C114) is reasonable but speculative. The high failure rate and limited slice number indicate this is not the optimal approach but validates the robustness of the biological observations.

result: Fixed (4% paraformaldehyde) mouse heart tissue imaged by serial pFIB/SEM revealed sarcomeres (average length 1.68 µm) with visible Z-disc, I-band, A-bands, and putative M-line, organized between mitochondrial columns. The volume (2698.4 µm³) contained 997 mitochondria, giving a concentration of 0.36 mitochondria/µm³, consistent with previous observations in mouse heart.
evaluation: Claims C115-C124 demonstrate application to fixed tissue with detailed structural observations. The sarcomere length measurement (C119) is quantitative with appropriate statistics (SD, N). The mitochondrial concentration (C123) agrees with prior literature (C124), validating the quantitative analysis. The use of fixation (C116) is justified for practical reasons. The detailed visualization of sarcomere components (C118) demonstrates resolution capability.

result: FRC-based resolution assessment across datasets showed sample-dependent variation (brain vs HeLa despite identical parameters; R. rubrum vs Vero twofold difference) reflecting importance of focusing, astigmatism, and sample variability. No resolution degradation was observed during acquisition series, even in long runs (500 slices).
evaluation: Claims C125-C128 provide systematic resolution assessment across multiple samples. The observation of sample-dependent variation (C126-C127) is important for understanding technique limitations. The lack of resolution degradation over time (C128) demonstrates stability. However, the FRC method's calibration and patch size choices could affect absolute values. The comparative analysis is more robust than absolute resolution claims.

result: Lamellae of R. rubrum and RPE-1 cells were prepared using serial pFIB/SEM (200 pA) followed by final polishing (60 pA) and imaged by both SEM and TEM. Features could be correlated between modalities despite physical differences arising from imaging depth (SEM: ~25 nm surface, TEM: entire 300 nm thickness). Fluorescence from chlorophyll was correlated with both pFIB/SEM and TEM images.
evaluation: Claims C129-C138 demonstrate compatibility with downstream cryo-ET workflows. The correlation between SEM and TEM (C131, C136) validates the approach. The explanation of differences (C132-C135) based on imaging physics is sound. The multimodal correlation including fluorescence (C137) is particularly valuable. The conclusion (C138) that serial pFIB/SEM is suitable for correlative workflows is well-supported, though potential ion damage effects are not fully addressed here.

result: Charging artefacts, occurring in lipid-rich regions and manifesting as dark spots with asymmetric streaks, were computationally mitigated using U-Net segmentation of charge centers followed by row-by-row filtering. Automated segmentation achieved 0.93 Dice coefficient compared to manual cleanup, indicating minimal manual intervention needed. Overall image resolution remained unchanged after charge removal.
evaluation: Claims C139-C146 describe a practical solution to a significant technical challenge. The physical basis for charging (C139) is established. The computational approach (C142-C143) is clearly described with quantitative validation (C144). The high Dice coefficient (C144) supports the claim of minimal manual intervention (C145). The preservation of resolution (C146) is important. However, the method cannot recover information in the charged region itself, which is appropriately acknowledged.

result: Automated segmentation of mitochondria in heart tissue using SuRVos2 achieved 0.87 Dice score compared to manual segmentation, with volume percentages in agreement (24% automated vs 20% manual). Component counts differed (15 automated vs 23 manual after filtering), demonstrating feasibility of automated segmentation but requiring additional work to quantify errors.
evaluation: Claims C147-C151 demonstrate proof-of-concept for automated analysis. The Dice score (C148) indicates good agreement. The volume percentage agreement (C149) is encouraging. The discrepancy in component counts (C150) is honestly reported and highlights remaining challenges. The conclusion (C151) appropriately characterizes this as a baseline demonstration rather than a fully validated method. Additional validation would strengthen this result.

result: All four gases (O, N, Ar, Xe) can produce smooth surfaces under some conditions, with behavior depending on ion current and voltage. Monatomic gases (Ar, Xe) are speculated to be less reactive and less prone to curtaining. Argon was selected as optimal for automated procedures based on low curtaining at low current and better performance at high currents, despite diatomic gases showing high automation failure rates (>80% vs <10% for argon).
evaluation: Claims C156-C164 synthesize the gas comparison results into practical recommendations. The observation that all gases can work under some conditions (C156) is important. The speculation about monatomic gases (C158) is clearly identified as such. The selection of argon (C164) is well-justified by the data. The quantitative comparison of failure rates (C162) strongly supports the choice. The discussion of prior work with oxygen (C163) provides context.

result: Prior work showed Ar plasma (30 kV, 60 pA) adversely affected ribosome resolution within ~45 nm of surface despite smooth surfaces, attributed to ion damage. For serial pFIB/SEM, argon wattage is twofold higher (200 pA at 20 kV vs 60 pA at 30 kV). Nitrogen showed higher resolution than argon in comparative imaging, suggesting damage may depend on plasma type and not simply correlate with curtaining, but further investigation is required.
evaluation: Claims C165-C171 raise important concerns about potential damage but lack direct experimental validation in this study. The citation of prior work (C165-C167) is appropriate. The inference about lack of correlation between curtaining and damage (C168) is logical. The observation that nitrogen showed higher resolution than argon (C170) is intriguing but based on limited comparison. The speculation (C171) is appropriately cautious. This represents an important limitation requiring future work.

result: SEM imaging dose was under 10⁻² e⁻/Å² over the whole scanned image, lower than cryo-ET imaging doses. SEM-induced damage would be expected to be confined to the interaction depth (<50 nm), contained within the same volume as FIB damage (~45 nm near the surface).
evaluation: Claims C172-C174 provide important dosimetry information. The comparison to cryo-ET doses (C173) with citation provides context. The inference about damage localization (C174) is reasonable based on electron interaction physics and supported by citation. However, this is theoretical expectation rather than direct measurement of damage in this study. The low dose is reassuring for the technique's viability.

result: Cryo-serial pFIB/SEM enables mesoscale imaging (10 nm to 10 µm) of vitrified samples while maintaining hydration shells for downstream structural biology. Despite challenges of low contrast, curtaining, and charging, an automated workflow produced 3D volumes of bacteria, cells, and tissue with 20-50 nm resolution. The approach is highly controllable, relatively rapid, laboratory-based, and compatible with subsequent imaging modalities.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C29-C32, and C175-C178 represent the overarching conclusions of the study. The technical challenges (C3) were systematically addressed through the work. The resolution achievement (C4) is supported by multiple datasets. The range of samples (C32) demonstrates versatility. The advantages listed (C178) are supported by the experimental results. The conclusion that this is a useful addition to structural biology (C175-C176) is well-justified by the comprehensive demonstration across multiple biological systems.

result: Background and motivation: Current FIB/SEM is almost exclusively applied to fixed, stained samples. Cryo-ET requires thin lamellae (<300 nm) typically prepared with Ga+ FIB. Current targeting approaches (cryo-CLEM, soft X-ray tomography) have limitations. Plasma FIB offers higher currents than Ga+ for faster ablation. Biological SEM imaging is challenging due to low contrast from light atoms, traditionally addressed by fixation/staining which precludes near-atomic resolution analysis. Imaging at crossover energies can reduce charging.
evaluation: Claims C5-C28 establish the context and rationale for the study. These are primarily literature-based knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations. The identification of technical challenges (C3, C12, C21-C23) and limitations of existing approaches (C13, C15-C16, C25-C26) clearly motivates the development of cryo-serial pFIB/SEM. The technical background on plasma FIB (C18-C20) and SEM physics (C27-C28) is accurate.

result: Initial imaging parameters were established: 52° SEM angle, 50 nm milling step (compromise between workflow and electron interaction depth of 30-90 nm), imaging at 1.1-1.2 kV with 6.3-13 pA current, 100 ns dwell time with 50-100 line integration. Depth of field was ~20 µm at both 1 and 2 kV, requiring focus correction after ~400 slices at 50 nm step thickness.
evaluation: Claims C51-C56 and C89-C90 describe methodological optimization with clear rationale. The milling step choice (C52) balances practical and physical considerations based on cited literature (C53-C54). The imaging parameters (C55-C56) are empirically optimized. The depth of field measurement (C89) with practical implication (C90) is useful for experimental planning. These represent important technical details for reproducibility.
